# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

## Respondents

Practitioners (primary link, `finance_lead`):
- Dana Whitfield: HN/47279411 ("we wouldn't want to switch even for a higher yield… the operational burden is more important to us than yield", "about 3.2%"). The $300k transfer is **[author]**.
- Marcus Oyelaran: HN/47279219 (self-directed brokerage, "more paperwork and back and forth", then "click that button now!"). The $3M and August are **[author]**.
- Lena Hofstra: HN/47279349 ("nowhere near juicy enough for me to literally bet the company on") and HN/47279304 (bank-run worry). The Treasuries-only policy and the two banks are **[author]**, after the 2023 bank failures the thread refers to.
- Tomás Reyes: HN/47283895 ("I’ve wanted this produce for years"), with the launch post's "large infusion from a raise". Cash sitting in plain checking is **[author]**.
- Aisha Karimi: HN/47279292 ("business savings accounts not much below this (2.85%) while keeping things safe (FDIC insured)").
- Ben Okafor: HN/47280707 (the fee "peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less"). The $1.5M is **[author]**.
- Rachel Lindqvist: HN/47282512 and HN/47283590 (PHC and QSBS: "a bunch of startups are raising $20m on $0 revenue … interest … can easily be the only income").
- Hiro Tanabe (gate No): HN/47279242 ("Startups otherwise are lean and won't hold enough cash to get a meaningful return").
- Grace Mbeki: HN/47283265 ("they might be better suited to deal with a fractional CFO service"). The Slack approval is **[author]**; the YC page (YCC) says the firm is reachable around the clock on Slack (paraphrased).
- Owen Castellano (chip): author's invention, filling a gap: no commenter refuses to say. A chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person. It loosely echoes HN/47279377 (an investor steering portfolio companies).
- Nadia Seferović: HN/47286820 ("ask your bank manager for rates on a 30 day deposit account … it appeared in my online banking the next day").
- Kevin Duarte: the launch post ("a mutual fund where your principal is at considerable risk – it had a 9% loss in 2022") and HN/47280944 (the short-term bond fund in "one of the leading startup treasury products"). Moving the loss to August 2026 is **[author]**.

Decision-makers (`link: COMMERCIAL_B2B`, `founder`, Part 3 only, no story on screen):
- Sofia Marchetti: author's invention, filling a gap: the thread has almost no willing buyer. She stands for the founders' own case ("putting $5M into Palus yields them an extra $50k-75k per year", HN/47290584) and the batchmates who "wanted this too" (HN). Her $2,000 a month is the bank's treasury fee.
- Jamal Booker: HN/47297953 ("That 50-75k is more like $5k/month out of what is typically a ~200-400k monthly burn") and HN/47401784 ("it definitely takes weeks to diligence").
- Eleanor Vance: HN/47279349 ("bet the company"); the board having to agree is **[author]**.
- Ravi Menon: HN/47279377 ("I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries"). The investor who had to agree is his.
- Maya Feldman: HN/47283895 (signed up) and HN/47283356 (liked "a number that goes up").
- Daniel Osei: HN/47283590 ("The probability is Low but the impact for us is massive"). The tax adviser's long sign-off is his.
- Irene Kowal: HN/47279831 ("This should be a hard pass for literally everyone … SGOV") and HN/47279261 ("just put the money in a Bond ETF").
- Felix Brandt: HN/47282750 ("I am willing to take a little bit more risk for a higher return … an extra month or two of runway").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: The fee-eats-the-gain answers sit together, the 'bank already pays us, why bother' answers sit together, the two names are plain and distinct, and Ravi's board-approval story fits neither group, so leaving it on its own is right.
whys.g2: There is no junk or explicit answer on this line; Ravi's answer drifts off price but was kept out of the groups rather than forced into one.

founder.order_why: The flow runs well from context through problem, idea and how it sells, but 'How should founders answer?' (24) comes after the interviews are marked sent, when it should be settled before anything goes out.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the identical context question; the commitment step (20, my 'start small, try us out') and 'Offer a pilot?' (22) ask nearly the same thing.
founder.missing: A way to price as a share of the balance (0.25% a year on AUM) rather than a fixed monthly amount, and the reserve size that monthly figure assumes; an advantage of 'more yield / more runway' rather than the nearest of the five codes; whether the cost today is yield given up or money spent, since my cost is foregone interest, not fees; and a minimum idle-cash balance below which the offer does not apply.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It goes from what idle cash cost me, to what I'd pay, to who signs and what diligence it needs, to whether I'd move money, which is how I'd actually think it through, though the counter jumps from 2 of 6 to 4 of 6 with no 3.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: What I use for idle cash today (we already pay the bank's treasury sweep about $2,000 a month) and what would make me switch; how safe the money is (FDIC or sweep coverage, Treasuries vs money-market, counterparty risk); and how fast I can pull it back to operating when payroll or a big bill hits.

screens.why3: I know who signs off on where a startup's reserve sits, because the thread itself raised the board and the investor, so I can answer from what I know.
screens.why4: A free box of up to 25 words with one escape chip, "Leave this out of the study", fits a typed answer, and nothing is missing or doubled.
screens.why5: I typed "The board", but Keel's belief says "nobody else must agree first", which is the opposite of what I said.
screens.why7: This is the card's bad example exactly: a typed role (the board) read as nobody else, so strangers who say the board would have to agree, which is my own answer, would count against me.
screens.instead: Keep the question and box as they are, but make the belief read: The startup founder decides, and the board must agree first.

screens.why1: Right after I named the board as having to agree, it makes sense to check the people Keel wrote down before it fixes the belief for Part 3.
screens.why2: The words are mine, but the board row has no tag next to it, and the belief says nobody else must agree. I had to read it twice to see whether Keel had counted the board at all.
screens.why3: Who runs the cash, who signs where the reserve sits, and whether the board has to agree is something I know from my own company.
screens.why4: The roles are the ones I named and none are added, but 'The board' has no tag (it should say 'has to agree'), and the casing is uneven ('finance lead' next to 'Startup founder').
screens.why5: I typed 'The board' as having to agree, and the belief turned it into 'nobody else must agree first'. That is the opposite of what I said.
screens.why7: This is the card's bad example: a typed role read as 'nobody else'. Strangers who say the board would have to agree, which is my own answer, would be counted against me, so the belief cannot be tested as I said it.
screens.instead: Rows: finance lead · has the problem / Startup founder · decides to buy / The board · has to agree; belief: The startup founder decides, and the board must agree first.

screens.why1: Right after I named the board as having to agree, asking whether I test that or the founder alone is the obvious next step before Part 3.
screens.why2: The choice itself is plain, but the bar's 'the last time they bought managing the money they will not touch' is clumsy; I'd say 'moved the reserve into a treasury product', and 'Pick the one role' sits oddly when one option is 'Nobody else'.
screens.why3: Whether my founders sign off on where the reserve sits alone or need the board is exactly what I know from the batch and the HN thread.
screens.why4: The two options are complete and distinct and keep my own 'The board', but 'Nobody else' should come first, not second, and the intro calls it a role.
screens.why5: 'The board' is kept word for word and my pick of 'Nobody else' is tested as picked, but Keel's 'managing the money they will not touch' stands in for my treasury product and is not my wording.
screens.why7: The measure and balance hold (Nobody else tested: decided alone for, the three wider answers against, at 2 in 3), but the shape is bent: Nobody else is not fixed first, and the bar uses the past 'last time they bought' form though this is the decision-maker's link, where the card asks 'Could you sign off on ... yourself'.
screens.instead: Which do you want to test? Nobody else (the founder signs off alone) · The board (the founder decides, the board must agree first). Bar: holds if at least 2 in 3 founders say they could sign off on about 0.25% of the reserve a year themselves.

screens.why1: Right after I named who else has to agree, it makes sense to ask what slows the purchase, and diligence, board sign-off and tax review are the brakes I see when founders move a reserve.
screens.why2: Approvals, reviews, procurement and switching are words any founder who has bought a finance product uses, and 25 words is enough for my three steps.
screens.why3: I know how a founder's own diligence, board policy and tax adviser hold up moving cash out of Mercury or Brex treasury, because I lived it with our own reserve.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with one escape, Leave this out of the study, which is the right way out for a founder who can't name a step.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my first step word for word, diligence on a new provider, and keeps founders as the deciders.
screens.why7: The steps fit the card: three of them, on the buyer's side, in my words, the biggest blocker first, and none is my own pitch; but the belief shown has no time in it yet, so as written it does not have the founder's time it will be tested against.
screens.instead: What could slow down or stop a purchase? (Approvals, reviews, procurement, switching. Up to 25 words.) You'll pick the biggest one next and say how long you think it takes.

screens.why1: Right after I named what slows a purchase, checking the list Keel kept is the obvious next step before I pick one and give its time.
screens.why2: Board approval of the cash policy, diligence on a new provider and a tax adviser's sign-off are how founders and finance leads talk about moving a reserve.
screens.why3: These are the real gates I hear about from batchmates and investors before a company moves its reserve out of the bank's treasury.
screens.why4: Three distinct buyer-side brakes, all mine, none overlapping, none my own offer or onboarding, with the board's sign-off first as the biggest blocker.
screens.why5: All three rows are exactly the steps I typed, kept in my words, with nothing added or merged.
screens.why7: The rows meet the card's shape, but the belief has already picked diligence (not the first, biggest row) before I chose one, and it carries no time, so as written it cannot be tested on the duration scale until the Choose screen supplies my pick and my time.
screens.instead: Same three rows, with the belief left blank until I pick a step and type its time: 'Most startup founders would get through [the step I pick] within about [my time], or not need it.'

screens.why1: Right after I listed what could slow a purchase and checked Keel's copy, picking the one step to test, with my own time, is the obvious next move.
screens.why2: The steps are my own words and plain to me, but the screen tests two bars that disagree: the box says 'under your time or not needed' while Keel will test says 'quick or not needed', and 'before it went through' is odd for a diligence or a tax sign-off.
screens.why3: I know how long a board takes to approve a cash policy and how long a CFO's diligence on a new custodian runs, because I've lived both from the other side.
screens.why4: These are my three steps, word for word, each a separate brake on the buyer's side. Board approval is first as the biggest blocker, there is no padded Keel row, and 'I'm not sure' is the right escape for my side.
screens.why5: The step I picked is kept exactly, but the belief has drifted: it says 'would get through diligence on a new provider' with no 'within about' my time, and 'quick' stands in for a number I never gave.
screens.why7: My time is null and the belief and bar still render, as 'quick' with no edge, so the duration scale has no working rung for strangers' bands to split on. The intro also asks 'before it went through', which the card names as a pitfall.
screens.instead: Which step do you want to test? [Board approval of the cash policy · Diligence on a new provider · A tax adviser's sign-off] -- How long do you think it takes them? [__] [days/weeks/months] (or I'm not sure) -> Keel will test: Most startup founders would get through diligence on a new provider within about 4 weeks, or not need it; with no test shown until I type a time or pick 'I'm not sure'.

screens.why1: After who decides, the friction and the setup time, asking what first step I'd want a founder to take is the obvious next question, and the frame says it is the last commercial one.
screens.why2: 'First real step' and 'costs them time, data, money or a signature' are plain to me, and 'the reserve' is how we talk about a startup's long-term cash.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I'd ask for first, because I already tell people to 'start small, try us out, and grow your position over time'.
screens.why4: The only chip is 'Leave this out of the study', which fits the founder's side of this card (I'm not sure leaves the dimension out) and does not overlap the typed box.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my words, 'move a small part of the reserve', with the founder as the one who decides, and adds no 'now', timing or number I didn't write.
screens.why7: The step is on the one measure (what they'd actually do before paying), in base form after 'would', under nine words, with the founder deciding, but one rule is bent: the hint allows 25 words where the card caps the step at 9, and neither the hint nor the belief makes the step say where the money goes (into Palus), so a stranger's 'Yes, I'd move a small part of the reserve' could mean anywhere.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take, saying where the money goes? Up to 9 words, e.g. 'move a small part of the reserve into Palus'.

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first real step, it makes sense that Keel shows me how strangers will hear it before the commercial section closes.
screens.why2: 'Move a small part of the reserve' is how a founder talks about their raise money, so I read it at once.
screens.why3: Deciding whether to move some of the reserve is a call I make as founder-CEO, so a founder can answer it from their own life.
screens.why4: The step never says where the money goes: 'move a small part of the reserve' could mean another bank, a T-bill ladder or SGOV, so a yes does not have to be a yes to us, and no smaller free step sits beside it even though this step costs the founder money.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'start small' but drops the destination, so it drifts from what I meant: move a small part of the long-term reserve into Palus.
screens.why7: The step is one measure with a Probably / Probably not / No set the card fixes, so the belief can hold or fail, but it breaks one shape rule (the step must name where the money goes), and with no smaller step 'Probably yes' stands alone even though the step costs money.
screens.instead: Step: 'move a small part of the reserve into Palus' (smaller step: 'the five-minute setup, with no money moved'), so strangers hear 'Yes, I'd move a small part of the reserve into Palus · Probably, after the five-minute setup with no money moved first · Probably not · No'.

screens.why1: At the last step before strangers see the study, asking whether to collect emails from those who would try it is the obvious place, and it follows straight from the commitment step I just set: start small with part of the reserve.
screens.why2: 'Offer a pilot?' with the exact line strangers will see and where I find the yeses is plain on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want sign-ups from finance leads is my own call, and it matches what I did at launch: 'start small, try us out, and grow your position over time'.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for this choice, and no escape is needed for a founder's own decision.
screens.why5: My picked Yes and my step, 'move a small part of the reserve', stand as I typed them; the generic 'try this for real' line does not misstate the offer.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs in the last step before the link goes out, after the study itself is settled.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint says Keel records a 'voice' for a video interviewer, so I am unsure whether I am picking a voice or a face, and '400 credits' is Keel's own unit rather than a price I can read.
screens.why3: I can play two five-second clips and decide which one my people would take a call from.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers, each with a sample to hear, the default marked; nothing overlaps and nothing is missing for a choice of voice.
screens.why5: It says the interviewer asks 'finance leads', but my study also sends Part 3 to founders who decide where the reserve sits, and that half of my audience is dropped from the question.
screens.instead: Who should ask finance leads and founders your questions? (Daphne ▶ hear / Saskia ▶ hear): the face and voice they will see on video, 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks finance leads, it is obvious I next pick how the founders who decide on the reserve will answer their part, before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Daphne, read and tap, and let them choose are each explained in one plain line I can pick from on first reading.
screens.why3: I know founders at funded startups live in Slack and email and would rather tap through on their phone than sit for a video, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete (voice, text, or their choice), and no escape chip is needed for a setup choice.
screens.why5: It names founders, the decision-maker role I set for Part 3, and my pick of Read and tap is kept.

screens.why1: Once the questions are set and the founders' answer mode is chosen, choosing who receives the links is the obvious last step before anything goes out.
screens.why2: Every option is in plain words: a link per person I know, a list from Keel's Contacts page, or one open link posted where people already gather, such as our YC batch's channels.
screens.why3: I know who I would reach: batchmates and founders and finance leads I know by name, so I can answer this without guessing.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would actually reach people, and posting one open link in a founder community is a real alternative to named links.
screens.why5: My study has two groups, finance leads for Parts 1 and 2 and founders for Part 3, and 'Who gets a link?' doesn't say which group this choice covers, so it drifts a little from what I set up.
screens.instead: Who gets a link, the finance leads and the founders? (same three options, chosen per group: people I know by name / a list from Contacts / one open link posted where they already are)

screens.why_b1: The headline 'Not holding up' sits beside its number (1 of 7 lose 2% or more), but the page says the verdict is the worst card, and Commitment's 'Did not hold' reads worse than 'Not holding up', so I can't tell why Existing sacrifice is the deciding one.
screens.why_b2: Each card's 'x of n · bar y of n' line reads quickly, but the kicker's '1 TO 8 COUNTED' takes a second look, and Purchase friction shows '1 counted' out of 8 answers with no reason given.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment are my lines word for word, but Existing sacrifice became '2% of the balance' on 'the operating account', when my estimate was the yield given up in the bank's treasury product (about 1 to 1.5% on $5M).
screens.why_b4: The cards say 'smaller than you think' and 'they value it below your price', but nothing tells me what to change: the fee, who I sell to, or whether to lead with a small first move.
screens.why_b5: Every card keeps its n and bar visible, the two thin ones are called too few to call, and nothing is called strong.
screens.instead: Lead with the one that did not hold (only 4 of 8 founders would move even a small part of the reserve) and say what to try next, e.g. a smaller first step or answering the board's and diligence worries; and say Existing sacrifice counted fees, not the yield founders give up.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Not holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 1 of 7 at 2% or more against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know at once that the belief failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 7 counted and the cells split 1 for and 6 against. But the card uses 'your bar' for two things, my 2% on the 0-3 percent axis and the 5-of-7 marker on the strip, and it took me a second look to tell which was which.
screens.why_b3: I can recognise it as my idle-cash cost, but my own estimate was yield given up of about $4,000 to $6,000 a month on a $4M to $6M reserve. Here it is restated as '2% of the balance per company a year' on the operating account alone, which is a reworded version of my number, not the one I typed.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats the count and points to the Price card. It never says what this means for Palus, for example that my pitch has to show the yield gap on the reserve, not on the operating account, or that the cost case is weak for founders who already use a bank treasury.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (8 answered, 7 counted, Ravi set apart, 2 none counted as 0), and the screen says plainly 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so nothing claims more than 7 founders can carry.
screens.instead: Not holding up, a lean from 7 founders: only 1 of 7 put the interest they missed at 2% of the balance or more, and most put it under 1% or at none. Lead the pitch with the dollar gap on the reserve, about $50k a year on $5M, not a percent of the operating account.

screens.why_b1: The verdict is plain: Not holding up, they value it below my price. The deciding count, 1 of 8 at 0.25% or more against a bar of 6 of 8, sits right under it.
screens.why_b2: Each band is labelled with its count and for or against, my 0.25% is marked as the low edge of its band, and the strip shows 1 for, 7 against and the marker at 6, so all three read on first look.
screens.why_b3: The flat 0.25% on AUM is recognisably my fee, but 'of the balance per company a year' adds a 'per company' unit I never charge by, and 'fair' is Keel's word, not mine.
screens.why_b4: It names the cluster at 0.1% to under 0.25% but stops there and sends me to Insights; it never says plainly that a fee nearer what Mercury or Rho already charge is where these founders would look.
screens.why_b5: All 8 answers are shown and counted, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing is claimed beyond the eight founders.
screens.instead: Not holding up: 1 of 8 founders would pay 0.25% or more on the balance a year, and most put a fair fee at 0.1% to under 0.25%, at or below what their bank's treasury already takes, so test a fee under the bank's or lead with the after-fee yield.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside the number that decides it, '1 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', so I know nothing was decided and why.
screens.why_b2: The strip is plain (1 counted, 4 ghost cells, bar at 4 of 5), but the chart's bare axis '0 0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5' has no label, so I have to look twice to work out what it is plotting.
screens.why_b3: The name is right, but I never checked 'lose at least that much of the balance today, so it is paid out of the gain'; Keel derived it from my cost and price, and the card shows it as 'Your belief' without saying Keel wrote it.
screens.why_b4: 'Ability to pay waits until 5 have' is generic: it doesn't say what actually blocks it, which is that 7 of 8 founders priced below 0.25% or wouldn't pay at all, so price is the problem to fix first.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said ('a lean, not a call'), but the question asked is the budget one ('where would the money come from?') while the rule and Maya's row read 'loses your price or more' next to what is her price band, which implies a cost of hers the screen never shows.
screens.instead: Not called: only Maya Feldman of 8 founders named 0.25% or more (7 named less or wouldn't pay), so ability to pay can't be read until the price holds. Fix the price, or test a lower fee, before asking where the money comes from. (This belief is Keel's, derived from your cost and price.)

screens.why_b1: The number is right beside the verdict (5 of 8 could sign alone, bar 6 of 8, 1 short), but the status word 'People disagree' never says whether my belief held, and the line under it ('of the 3 against, 2 said...') reads as a fragment rather than a verdict.
screens.why_b2: At first look I can see what is counted (who could sign alone), over how many (8), and where the bar sits (a marker at 6 against 5 for and 3 against).
screens.why_b3: The card is 'Buyer and payer', and the belief is word for word the one I checked: 'The startup founder decides, and nobody else must agree first.'
screens.why_b4: 'Expect someone else's agreement in some deals' points the right way, but it sends 'who' to another tab, when the people on this screen (one investor-style 'several people', two 'someone else') could already tell me to plan for board or investor sign-off.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (8 answered, 8 counted), the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than 5 of 8.
screens.instead: Not holding, 1 short: 5 of 8 founders could sign alone (bar 6); 3 needed someone else, so build board or investor sign-off into your pitch.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right above its number, "1 counted · 5 needed to call it", and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts only the 1 founder who gave a length (0 / 0 / 1), but the strip's "4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3 say quick or not needed)" mixes a count bar with a share bar, and the 7 who couldn't tell are missing from the chart, so I had to look twice to see it is over 1 person, not 8.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Purchase friction and carries my belief word for word: most startup founders would get through diligence on a new provider, or not need it.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic: it never says that 7 of 8 founders couldn't say whether diligence would even be needed, which is itself the thing I need to act on (they have no picture of what moving the reserve involves), nor what to ask or show next.
screens.why_b5: The count stays visible and the low n is said, but calling a single founder's answer "a lean" is a soft overstatement, since one person leans nothing.
screens.instead: 7 of 8 founders couldn't tell whether a new provider would need diligence, so they don't yet know what moving the reserve involves. Only 1 gave an answer, too few to call; show them what your diligence pack covers, and ask how many weeks they'd expect it to take.

screens.why_b1: 'Did not hold' sits right beside '4 of 8 said yes, bar 6 of 8, 2 short', so I know the verdict and the number that decides it at once.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 8 founders, all 8 counted, and the strip puts the marker at 6 against 4 for, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are plain.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and 'In most cases the startup founder would move a small part of the reserve' are exactly the belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates that 4 of 8 would not move a small part and sends me to the Insights tab; it doesn't tell me what this means for the idea, e.g. that half the founders won't even pilot with a slice of the reserve, so the five-minute setup pitch isn't the blocker and trust or diligence is.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, the count line says it is a small group and a lean rather than a call, and nothing claims more than the 4 for and 4 against.
screens.instead: Half of 8 founders wouldn't move even a small part of the reserve (2 flat no), so trust, not setup effort, is what to fix before asking for money; see Insights for what they named.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict (Not holding up, People disagree, Did not hold) with the deciding count and bar beside it, such as 1 of 8 at 0.25% or more against a bar of 6 of 8, and the count lines add up.
screens.why_b3: The Buyer and payer and Commitment belief lines are word for word the ones I checked, and the Price line is my 0.25% fee in my terms.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what to do with the idea; I have to work out for myself that the fee is being judged against the extra yield and that the board wants a say.
screens.why_b5: Every box keeps its n and its against count visible, the empty boxes say plainly that nobody was asked their why there, and nothing claims more than the answers carry.
screens.why_b6: One new framing, that a quarter percent eats too much of a one point gain, is worth having, but the rest repeats the HN sceptics I already built into my sources, and the two boxes whose whys I most needed (who must agree, what they'd start with) are empty.
screens.instead: Say that founders judge the fee against the extra yield, not the balance, so I should price on the spread or show yield after fees; and show Ravi's and Daniel's board quotes under Buyer and payer, where they actually answer my belief that nobody else must agree.

screens.why1: As the very first thing I hear, an idea pitched cold before anyone has asked whether I even hold raise cash at a bank is abrupt, though it plainly sets up the buying questions.
screens.why2: Plaid, custodian, money market fund and checking are my world, but 'government-backed mortgage bonds, short-duration and floating-rate' is a bond-desk phrase I would have to read twice and would never say myself.
screens.why3: I decide where our raise sits and I know roughly what our bank's sweep fund pays, so I can weigh this against what we do today.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options, rows or box.
screens.why5: It is shown on purpose as an idea to imagine, and nothing reaches me beyond the product it describes, in terms a finance person would use.
screens.why6: Heard once, the how runs five sentences rather than one line, and 'short-duration and floating-rate' tacked onto the bonds is a mouthful I would lose before the yield line comes.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus, a treasury account that invests a startup's reserve. It links to your bank and holds your reserve in short-term, government-backed bonds in the company's name, back in checking in one to two business days. The people building it believe it would earn 4.5 to 5 percent a year, against about 3.5 percent in your bank's money market fund.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what idle cash in the operating account cost us last year is the obvious place to start the buying questions for someone who signs off on where the money sits.
screens.why2: I know what interest on the operating account means, but 'how much interest' makes me think in dollars, and only the label tells me it wants a percent of the balance, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I know roughly what our balance was and what a treasury account pays, but interest I 'missed' is a counterfactual, so I'd be working out a gap rather than recalling a number I saw.
screens.why4: The box, None and I can't recall cover me, but the stem asks 'how much' while the box wants a percent, so I'm not sure whether to type dollars or a rate.
screens.why5: Interest on cash sitting in the operating account is my own banking language, and nothing of the founder's product or its terms reaches me here.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, but 'how much interest' then 'a percent of the balance' is hard to hold when heard: I hear an amount and then have to switch to a rate.
screens.why7: The measure matches the founder's (a percent of the balance per year, so 2% can be placed for or against), and the one escape is there with None as an open point, but the verb 'miss' is the vague verb the card warns against instead of the thing I saw go.
screens.instead: Last year, about what percent of the balance did the cash in your operating account go without earning in interest? [ box ] % of the balance last year · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after I worked out the interest I left sitting in operating, asking what I'd pay to fix it is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: A yearly fee as a percent of the balance is how every treasury and sweep product I've looked at is priced, so I can answer it at once.
screens.why3: I sign off on where our cash sits and I've compared bank treasury fees, so I know what a fee on a few million would feel like to me.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct with no overlap and run from almost nothing to a full percent, and 'I wouldn't pay for this' and 'I can't say' cover the rest.
screens.why5: Only the idea card and the plain fee basis reach me, which is fair for a price question, and nothing reads like the company's own jargon.
screens.why6: Step one says well, but the fee sentence spoken before the question is a scene ahead of the stem, and 'a tenth to under a quarter of a percent' is a mouthful to hear once.
screens.why7: Every band is a percent of money I hold, a year, and there are five ascending bands, 'wouldn't pay' and one apart escape spoken 'Or say: I can't say', so a founder's fee somewhere in the range could be supported or refuted.
screens.instead: What yearly fee, as a percent of the cash Palus holds for you, would it be worth to you? Under 0.1% · 0.1% to under 0.25% · 0.25% to under 0.5% · 0.5% to under 1% · 1% or more · I wouldn't pay for this · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after I named a fee, asking what would make Palus worth paying more for is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: The question itself is plain, but it reads my pick back as the screen's band label, '0.1% to under 0.25%', instead of how I'd say it, 'about a tenth to a quarter of a percent'.
screens.why3: I know what I'd want for a higher fee: same-day liquidity, FDIC or Treasury safety, and no extra work for me or my controller.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: Palus and its yearly fee were already shown on the idea card and the price screen, so nothing new leaks, and it is in words I'd use.
screens.why6: Spoken aloud, '0.1% to under 0.25%' becomes 'zero point one percent to under zero point two five percent', a mouthful when §17 says a percent is said in words.
screens.instead: You said about a tenth to a quarter of a percent a year. What would make Palus worth paying more than that?

screens.why1: Right after the fee questions, it makes sense to ask whether I could approve moving our raise cash into Palus on my own or would need someone's agreement.
screens.why2: Sign off is how I talk about approving spend, so I can answer this on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly who has to bless a change to where our cash sits: me, plus maybe the board under our investment policy.
screens.why4: The four answers run from me alone to someone else's call, each is distinct, and I can't say is the one escape, set apart.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's own terms or roles leaks, only the product name Palus, which the idea card already showed me.
screens.why6: One short either-or question with four short spoken options and the escape said once at the end, which is easy to hold by ear.
screens.why7: The measure, order, four fixed answers with the anyone-else wording and the one I can't say escape all fit a Nobody else test, but the stem asks me to sign off on Palus rather than on the price, as the card asks.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on a fee of about 0.1% to 0.25% of the balance a year yourself, or would someone else have to agree? I could sign off myself · Someone else would have to agree · Several people would have to agree · It's someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: After asking whether I could sign off myself, asking what checks I'd run before moving our raise into Palus is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Diligence on a new provider is exactly the phrase I'd use for vetting where our cash sits, so I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I'm the one who'd vet a new treasury provider before moving money off Mercury, so I know what that review involves and roughly how long it runs.
screens.why4: The options are distinct and the escape fits, but 'a long time' versus 'quick' has no edge; for me a couple of weeks of checking a custodian and its insurance could be either.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's pitch or roles leaks through; it reads as my own step of vetting a provider.
screens.why6: It is one short question with three spoken options and one escape, easy to hold and answer by ear.
screens.why7: The step is a real buyer-side brake and the escape is right, but this is the old fixed three with no founder's time as a band edge, so 'long' is no one's number and the belief has no duration to hold or fail against.
screens.instead: If you bought Palus, how long would diligence on a new provider take? Bands around the founder's own time, then 'It wouldn't be needed', or 'I can't tell'.

screens.why1: This is the last of the buying questions, after price, sign-off and diligence, so asking whether I'd actually move money is the obvious close.
screens.why2: "Move a small part of the reserve" is how I'd talk about our cash, and I get it on first hearing, though I have to infer that it means moving it into Palus.
screens.why3: Deciding where our post-raise cash sits is my call, so I can answer straight from what I'd do.
screens.why4: There are four distinct answers, two firm and two soft, and the first one names the actual step, so my true answer is there.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the Palus card I was shown on purpose, and "a small part" keeps the term that makes this a low-risk ask.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four options read as a list I can hold, and nothing in it only the eye can read.
screens.why7: The measure, order, balance and no-escape rules all hold, with a firm and a soft yes against a firm and a soft no, but the step doesn't say where the money goes (into Palus), which the card asks the step to name.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you move a small part of the reserve into Palus, or not? Yes, I'd move a small part into Palus · Probably yes · Probably not · No
